title: The raft again (section 6)
hookLine: even the teaching is to be let go of, like a raft, and how much more what isn't the teaching

cards: Subhuti has a practical worry. He has just heard that a Buddha can't be seen by his marks.
So he asks what anyone who has explained something subtle to a skeptical friend might ask: in some later age, when people hear words like these, will anyone actually trust them?

The Buddha says yes, there will be such people. Then he reaches for a picture this path has met before, in the older discourses: a raft, built for a river, and the question of what to do with it once you're across.

teach.b: In a later time, the Buddha says, there will be people who keep the precepts, and when they hear even a single line of this teaching, a clear trust will arise in them.
Their roots of goodness, the sutra says, weren't planted with one Buddha only, but with countless Buddhas. Second, how they hold it.

They don't grab hold of teachings, and they don't grab hold of the denial of teachings either. Clutching the teaching is one ditch; clutching the idea that nothing matters is the other. Third, the raft.
That's why, the Buddha says, his teaching is to be understood as a raft. Even teachings are to be let go of, and how much more what isn't teaching. Fourth, the raft before this one.
In the Pali discourses, in a sutta called the Water Snake, a man facing a great flood binds grass, sticks and branches into a raft and paddles across.
On the far shore he wonders whether to hoist it onto his head and carry it with him, out of gratitude. No, the Buddha says. Leave it on the bank and go on.
The teaching is for crossing over, not for holding on to.

teach.h: EVEN THE TEACHING IS A RAFT.
teach.b: The Diamond Sutra pushes that old raft one step further: even the teaching itself, even this sutra.

teach.h: DON'T CARRY IT ON YOUR HEAD.
teach.b: Nobody throws the raft away in the middle of the river.
You need it on the water. The letting go comes when it has done its work.

how: Buddhist teachers in many schools use the raft picture to say that the teachings are tools for awakening, to be used fully and not clung to.

o: the teaching is a raft, let go of once it has carried you across
the teaching is a raft to throw away before you start
the teaching is a raft you should carry with you for life

games.q: the raft, twice: tap the pairs.
p: a man crosses a flood on a raft
leave the raft on the bank
even the teaching is let go of

s: the raft picture appears only in the Diamond Sutra
it's in the Pali Water Snake sutta too, where the man leaves the raft on the far bank.
the raft means you should drop the teaching before you cross
the raft is for crossing. it's let go of once it has done its work.
the sutra says people in a later age will still hear this with trust
even hearing a single line, a clear trust will arise in them.

games.q: you built a raft from grass and branches and crossed the flood on it. now you're on the far shore. what do you do with the raft?
o: carry it on your head, out of gratitude.
leave it on the bank and walk on.
break it apart so it can't be used again.
games.why: in the Water Snake sutta, the Buddha says leave it on the bank: the teaching is for crossing over, not for holding on to. the Diamond Sutra adds: even the teaching.

practice: Find one rule you've carried a long time, something that once got you across a hard stretch: never ask for help, always be early, keep the peace at any price.

Thank it, the way you might pat a raft that kept you dry, and ask: am I still on the river, or carrying this on my head? You don't have to decide; just set it on the bank for this sit, and breathe beside it.

wordCard.voice: The raft again. The teaching is a raft for crossing; even it is let go of, and how much more what isn't the teaching. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a teaching, and also a thing or phenomenon; the sutra says even dharmas are let go of, like a raft.

carryVoice: Your line: even the raft. A raft is for the river, not the road. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (the simile of the raft)
